title: Speedy's property income, Brooklyn life and Jones's list of piano teachers
summary: Their life near Ebbets Field; Andy Razaf's story of Fats Waller; and Jones's answer to Japanese interviewers about his teachers.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Did you know her after she came back (Inaudible) to New York?
Oh, yeah. No, after she came back to New York.
She went back to shows again? (Inaudible)

No, she didn't have to. She had the income from that property in Georgia. She didn't have to do a damned thing. She had a big, beautiful apartment. Well, her aunt had died on her mother's side, you know, and she was the only heir to receive this. She just didn't -- she didn't have to work. And eventually the mortgages and things, they ran out, you know, but they served their purpose, because it did a whole lot for me when I was sick, because I didn't work. I couldn't work, you know. And she didn't work. And we had a nice house out on Long Island at that point. But we used to have a lot of fun in Brooklyn. We had a nice house in Brooklyn. But we lived in Ebbet's Field with the Dodgers all the time. And it used to drive us up the wall, you know? I think after they moved out here they got more organized, but the Brooklyn bums were something. But we had a lot of fun with sports, you know? Baseball games and things.
Do you know where her apartment was located (Inaudible).
No. No. That's before I met her, you know. I never did try to -- well, you know, I just never thought I would have to know.

Yeah. No, Andy Razaf was the one -- we were paying a visit to him out here. He lived on Country Club Drive, and I think he was in a wheelchair by then, you know. And he was talking to me and talking to Speedy, you know, and then his wife, and he was telling me about it. Speedy didn't know. She didn't even know herself, you know. Fats used to go by, you know. I met Fats in Chicago once, and I used to idolize him. Well, he was one of the finest piano players that I knew, along with the history -- I think the Japanese people used to ask it in a certain way, when I'd go to Japan. They'd say, "Mr. Jones, who was your teacher?" Well, I would start as far back as James P. Johnston and Fats Waller, and then I would move up the line into Teddy Wilson, into Art Tatum, into Bud Powell, into Herbie Hancock. I'd say, "All these guys are my teachers, you know?" Chick Corea, you know. And all of it rubs off on you if you listen, you know? So they seemed to like that answer quite a bit.
